title: CLAUSES OF CONCESSION & REASON
notes:
✓ A clause of concession → shows contrast between two ideas, where one fact does not prevent another fact from being true.

✓ A clause of reason → explains why something happens or why someone does something.

◆ CONCESSION
Although, though, even though, even if, while, whereas, despite, in spite of.

◆ REASON
Because, since, as, because of, due to, owing to.

title: CLAUSES OF CONCESSION
notes:
✓ Concession expresses an unexpected contrast.

✓ Although it was raining, we went outside.
→ Rain normally prevents going outside, but we went anyway.

✓ Although he was tired, he continued working.

◆ BASIC PATTERN
Although/though/even though + subject + verb + main clause.

✓ Meaning → 'despite the fact that' or 'even though'.

title: ALTHOUGH
notes:
✓ Although → introduces a concessive clause and shows contrast.

✓ Although she was tired, she continued studying.
✓ He went to school although he was sick.

◆ PATTERN
Although + subject + verb.

✓ The clauses can be reversed:
Although it was expensive, I bought it.
I bought it although it was expensive.

✓ When the although-clause comes first, use a comma before the main clause.

title: THOUGH
notes:
✓ Though → has a similar meaning to although but is generally more common in informal speech.

✓ Though he was tired, he kept working.
✓ He kept working though he was tired.

✓ Though can also appear at the end of a sentence in informal English.

✓ The exam was difficult. I enjoyed it, though.

✓ This final-position use is different from the standard conjunction pattern.

title: EVEN THOUGH
notes:
✓ Even though → stronger than although and emphasizes the unexpected contrast.

✓ Even though he studied hard, he failed the exam.
✓ She went out even though it was raining heavily.

✓ Although → contrast.
✓ Even though → strong/unexpected contrast.

◆ PATTERN
Even though + subject + verb.

title: EVEN IF
notes:
✓ Even if → introduces a hypothetical or possible condition that will not change the result.

✓ Even if it rains, we will go.
✓ I will help you even if you make a mistake.

✓ Even though → refers to a fact or known situation.
✓ Even if → refers to a possibility or hypothetical situation.

✓ Even though he is poor, he is happy. → fact.
✓ Even if he becomes poor, he will be happy. → possibility.

title: DESPITE & IN SPITE OF
notes:
✓ Despite and in spite of → show concession but are normally followed by a noun, pronoun, or -ing form, not a complete clause.

✓ Despite the rain, we went outside.
✓ In spite of the rain, we went outside.
✓ Despite being tired, she continued working.
✓ In spite of his illness, he went to school.

◆ PATTERN
Despite + noun/-ing.
In spite of + noun/-ing.

✓ Despite does NOT take 'of'.
❌ despite of the rain
✓ despite the rain

title: DESPITE + CLAUSE
notes:
✓ To use despite/in spite of before a complete clause, use the fact that.

✓ Despite the fact that it was raining, we went out.
✓ In spite of the fact that he was tired, he continued working.

◆ COMPARE
✓ Although he was tired, he worked.
✓ Despite being tired, he worked.
✓ Despite the fact that he was tired, he worked.

title: WHILE & WHEREAS
notes:
✓ While and whereas can express contrast between two facts, situations, or people.

✓ While John is very outgoing, his brother is quiet.
✓ Whereas the old system was slow, the new system is faster.

✓ While → can mean contrast or time, so context matters.
✓ Whereas → specifically emphasizes contrast.

◆ PATTERN
While/whereas + subject + verb.

title: CLAUSES OF REASON
notes:
✓ A reason clause explains why an action or situation occurs.

◆ MAIN CONJUNCTIONS
Because, since, as.

✓ We stayed home because it was raining.
✓ Since you are here, you can help us.
✓ As I was tired, I went to bed early.

◆ PATTERN
Reason conjunction + subject + verb.

title: BECAUSE
notes:
✓ Because → gives a direct and clear reason.

✓ I stayed home because I was sick.
✓ She was late because the bus broke down.

✓ Because is the most direct and common way to introduce a reason clause.

✓ It can appear after or before the main clause.
We stayed home because it was raining.
Because it was raining, we stayed home.

✓ When the because-clause comes first, use a comma before the main clause.

title: SINCE & AS
notes:
✓ Since and as can introduce reasons, especially when the reason is already known, obvious, or less important than the main statement.

✓ Since you are tired, you should rest.
✓ As it was late, we went home.

✓ Because → usually stronger/more direct reason.
✓ Since/As → often introduce a background or already-known reason.

✓ Since can also mean 'from a time in the past until now', so context determines its meaning.

title: BECAUSE OF
notes:
✓ Because of → preposition followed by a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase.

✓ We stayed home because of the rain.
✓ He was absent because of his illness.
✓ The match was cancelled because of bad weather.

◆ PATTERN
Because of + noun/noun phrase.

✓ Do not normally follow because of directly with a full clause.

❌ We stayed home because of it was raining.
✓ We stayed home because it was raining.
✓ We stayed home because of the rain.

title: DUE TO & OWING TO
notes:
✓ Due to and owing to → formal expressions meaning 'because of'.

✓ The flight was delayed due to bad weather.
✓ The match was cancelled owing to heavy rain.

◆ PATTERN
Due to/owing to + noun phrase.

✓ Common in formal and academic writing.
✓ due to technical problems
✓ owing to financial difficulties
✓ due to heavy traffic

title: REASON: CLAUSE VS PHRASE
notes:
✓ Because + clause → subject + verb.
✓ The game was cancelled because it rained.

✓ Because of + noun phrase.
✓ The game was cancelled because of the rain.

✓ Due to + noun phrase.
✓ The game was cancelled due to the rain.

◆ REMEMBER
Because + subject + verb
Because of + noun/phrase
Due to + noun/phrase

title: CONCESSION: CLAUSE VS PHRASE
notes:
✓ Although/even though + clause.
✓ Although he was tired, he worked.

✓ Despite/in spite of + noun/-ing.
✓ Despite being tired, he worked.

✓ Despite/in spite of + the fact that + clause.
✓ Despite the fact that he was tired, he worked.

◆ REMEMBER
Although + subject + verb
Despite + noun/-ing
In spite of + noun/-ing

title: SENTENCE TRANSFORMATION
notes:
◆ CONCESSION
✓ Although he was sick, he went to school.
= Despite being sick, he went to school.
= In spite of his illness, he went to school.

◆ REASON
✓ We cancelled the trip because it was raining.
= We cancelled the trip because of the rain.

✓ The meaning stays the same, but the grammatical structure changes.

title: COMMON ERRORS
notes:
❌ Despite of the rain, we went out.
✓ Despite the rain, we went out.

❌ Despite it was raining, we went out.
✓ Although it was raining, we went out.
✓ Despite the fact that it was raining, we went out.

❌ Because of it was raining, we stayed home.
✓ Because it was raining, we stayed home.
✓ Because of the rain, we stayed home.

❌ Although of the rain, we went out.
✓ Although it was raining, we went out.

❌ Even though of his illness, he worked.
✓ Even though he was ill, he worked.

❌ Despite he was tired, he continued.
✓ Although he was tired, he continued.
✓ Despite being tired, he continued.

title: EXAM GUIDE
notes:
◆ 1. Contrast/unexpected result → concession.
◆ 2. Use although/though/even though + clause.
◆ 3. Use despite/in spite of + noun or -ing.
◆ 4. Use despite/in spite of + the fact that + clause.
◆ 5. Use even if for a hypothetical possibility.
◆ 6. Use because + subject + verb.
◆ 7. Use because of + noun/noun phrase.
◆ 8. Use since/as for reasons that are often known or background information.
◆ 9. Use due to/owing to + noun phrase in more formal contexts.
◆ 10. Check the difference between clause and phrase.

◆ QUICK MEMORY

⚖️ CONCESSION
Although + clause
Even though + clause
Though + clause
Even if + clause
Despite + noun/-ing
In spite of + noun/-ing

💡 REASON
Because + clause
Since + clause
As + clause
Because of + noun
Due to + noun
Owing to + noun

✓ Golden rule → Although/Because are followed by a clause; despite/because of/due to are followed by a noun, noun phrase, or appropriate -ing structure.
